title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS STILL ANOINT THE SICK WITH OIL? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH MANY BELIEVERS HAVE NEVER BEEN TAUGHT
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS STILL ANOINT THE SICK WITH OIL? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH MANY BELIEVERS HAVE NEVER BEEN TAUGHT

When the doctors have done everything they can, the prayers seem unanswered, and someone you love is suffering, does the Bible still tell us to reach for the oil? What James 5 actually teaches about healing, faith, suffering, and the God who has never stopped hearing His children.
There is a kind of silence that only exists in a hospital room.
The machines are still making noise. Nurses are walking through the hallway. Somewhere, a telephone is ringing.
But inside you, everything has gone quiet.
You are staring at someone you love, lying in a bed they never wanted to occupy. Perhaps it is your mother. Your father. Your spouse. Your child.
Or perhaps you are the one lying there.
You have prayed until you ran out of words. You have told God you trust Him, but somewhere beneath that confession is a question you are almost afraid to ask.
"Lord, are You going to heal me?"
Then someone from church arrives carrying a small bottle of olive oil.
They open their Bible to James chapter 5.
And suddenly, another question rises.

Does God actually command Christians to anoint sick people with oil today? Is this something the early church practiced that we have somehow forgotten? Does the oil have spiritual power? And if we pray and the person does not recover, does that mean somebody lacked faith?
These are not small questions.
Because behind them are real people. Real diagnoses. Real funerals. Real testimonies of healing. And believers who desperately want to honor God without believing something Scripture never promised.

So before anyone reaches for a bottle of oil, before anyone declares a miracle, and before anyone tells a suffering Christian that their faith is insufficient, we need to hear what the Bible actually says.
And the answer may be more beautiful, more sobering, and more Christ-centered than you expected.
The Bible really does instruct believers to pray over the sick and anoint them with oil.
But what Scripture says next is where we must listen carefully.
James 5:14–15 says:
"Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:
And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him."
That is the King James Version.
Notice what James does not say.
He does not say, "If anyone is sick, purchase a special bottle of oil from someone claiming to possess extraordinary spiritual power."
He does not say, "Find the most famous preacher you can."
He does not say, "If the person remains sick, accuse them of unbelief."
He tells the suffering believer to call for the elders of the church.
He tells the elders to pray.
He tells them to anoint the sick person with oil in the name of the Lord.
And he directs our attention to the Lord Himself.
That distinction changes everything.
Because biblical anointing is not about making oil powerful.
It is about depending upon the God who is powerful.
In the original Greek, James begins with a remarkably personal question:
Ἀσθενεῖ τις ἐν ὑμῖν;
Asthenei tis en hymin?
"Is anyone among you sick?"

The verb astheneō can describe weakness or illness, depending on context. Here, the reference to someone needing the elders to come and pray over them strongly supports the understanding that physical sickness is in view.
James is not writing to people who have never suffered.
He is writing to a community that knows weakness.
A community where someone may be too ill to gather with everyone else.
And rather than telling that person to suffer in isolation, he calls the church to come near.
Think about that.
God's instruction to a suffering Christian is not to hide until they become strong again.
It is to ask for help.
Somebody reading this needs to hear that.
You have been strong for everyone else for so long that asking someone to pray for you feels almost embarrassing.
You know how to encourage people.
You know how to quote Scripture.
You know how to smile at church while quietly wondering whether you can endure another week.
But James does not shame the weak believer for needing others.
He gives that believer permission to call.
To be vulnerable.
To say, "I need prayer."
And perhaps the first thing God wants to confront in some of us is not our sickness but our prideful insistence that we must carry every burden alone.
Now consider the oil itself.
The Greek expression in James 5:14 is:
ἀλείψαντες ἐλαίῳ
Aleipsantes elaiō.
"Having anointed with oil."

The verb aleiphō commonly refers to applying or rubbing oil onto someone. It differs from chriō, another Greek verb often associated with consecration or anointing, although we should not force an absolute theological distinction between the two words.
Oil was familiar in the ancient Mediterranean world.
It could be used for ordinary personal care, hospitality, and medicinal purposes. Luke 10:34 describes the Good Samaritan treating an injured man's wounds with oil and wine.
Oil also carried important associations with consecration and God's purposes throughout the Old Testament.
In Exodus 30, sacred anointing oil was associated with the consecration of priests and holy objects. In 1 Samuel 16:13, Samuel anointed David, and the Spirit of the Lord came upon him.
The Hebrew word commonly used for anointing is מָשַׁח (māšaḥ), from which the word māšîaḥ, or Messiah, is derived.
Messiah means "Anointed One."
In Greek, the corresponding title is Christos—Christ.
But we must be careful here.
James is not telling Christians to recreate Israel's sacred anointing-oil formula. Nor does he teach that ordinary olive oil becomes a supernatural substance merely because someone prays over it.
The connection between anointing and God's purposes is meaningful, but the text does not identify the oil as an independent source of healing.
In fact, James makes the source of healing unmistakable.
"And the Lord shall raise him up."
Not the oil.
Not the elder.
Not the eloquence of the prayer.
The Lord.
This is why Christians should never treat anointing oil like a spiritual charm.
A bottle of oil is not a substitute for repentance.
It is not a guarantee against disease.
It is not protection purchased through a ministry.
It cannot force God to perform a miracle.
And no amount of money can turn ordinary oil into divine authority.
The power belongs to God alone.
But someone may ask, "If the oil has no power of its own, why use it?"
Because obedience does not require us to believe that the physical object possesses supernatural power.
Water does not possess the power to forgive sins, yet baptism uses water as an important outward expression of Christian faith.
Bread and wine do not become spiritual bargaining chips, yet the Lord's Supper directs believers to remember Christ.
Likewise, anointing with oil can be a tangible expression of prayerful dependence upon God.
James explicitly includes it in his instruction.
We do not need to exaggerate its power to take his words seriously.
And we do not need to dismiss the practice simply because some people have abused it.
There is another passage many Christians overlook.
Mark 6:12–13 records what happened when Jesus sent out the Twelve:
"And they went out, and preached that men should repent.
And they cast out many devils, and anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them."
Notice the order.
They preached repentance.
They ministered to people suffering under demonic oppression.
They anointed many sick people with oil.
And healing occurred.
This is not a modern invention.
Anointing the sick with oil has clear biblical precedent in the ministry of Jesus' apostles.

However, Mark is describing a particular mission of the Twelve during Jesus' earthly ministry. We should not automatically assume every detail of that mission functions as a universal command for every believer in every situation.
James 5 is especially important because it gives direct instruction to the church about caring for the sick.
Taken together, these passages provide strong biblical grounds for Christians to practice prayerful anointing today.
Not as a performance.
Not as a commercial product.
Not as a ritual that guarantees a particular outcome.
But as an act of obedience, compassion, and dependence upon the Lord.
And now we reach the part of the passage that has wounded some believers more deeply than the sickness itself.
James says:
"And the prayer of faith shall save the sick."
What does that mean when the sick person dies?
What does it mean when the cancer returns?
What does it mean when the pastor prayed, the church fasted, the oil was applied, and the medical report still brought devastating news?
We cannot answer those questions by pretending they do not exist.
The Greek phrase is:
ἡ εὐχὴ τῆς πίστεως σώσει τὸν κάμνοντα
Hē euchē tēs pisteōs sōsei ton kamnonta.
"The prayer of faith will save the weary or sick person."
The verb sōzō can mean to save, rescue, or deliver, and in appropriate contexts it can refer to physical healing.
The word kamnō can convey weariness or exhaustion, and here it describes the person suffering.
James then says:
καὶ ἐγερεῖ αὐτὸν ὁ κύριος
Kai egerei auton ho kyrios.
"And the Lord will raise him up."
The language is genuinely hopeful. James expects believers to pray with confidence in God's ability to restore.
We should not weaken the passage until it means nothing more than, "Prayer might make you feel better."
James is speaking seriously about God's healing power.
But neither should we isolate his words from the rest of Scripture and turn them into an unconditional formula that guarantees immediate physical recovery whenever the correct ritual is performed.
Because the same Bible that tells us to pray for healing also shows us faithful servants of God who experienced suffering without immediate healing.
Consider Paul.
In 2 Corinthians 12:7–9, Paul describes a thorn in his flesh. Its exact nature is debated, so we should not confidently diagnose it as a particular illness.
But Paul tells us he pleaded with the Lord three times for it to depart.
And God's answer was:
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
Paul did not lack faith.
He was not secretly disqualified from God's love.
He was an apostle who pleaded for relief and received sustaining grace instead of the removal he requested.
Then consider Timothy.
Paul writes in 1 Timothy 5:23:
Timothy had recurring physical difficulties.
Paul did not simply accuse him of spiritual failure.
He offered practical advice appropriate to that historical setting.
This verse is not a general prescription to drink alcohol for medical problems today. It does show that practical care and faith in God need not oppose one another.
And in 2 Timothy 4:20, Paul writes:
Read that again.
Paul, through whom God had performed extraordinary miracles, left a fellow worker sick.
Scripture does not tell us why Trophimus had not recovered.
It does not authorize us to accuse him of unbelief.
It simply tells us the truth.
Faithful Christians can become sick.
Faithful Christians can remain sick.
And faithful Christians can die while trusting the Lord.
That reality does not cancel James 5.
It prevents us from turning James 5 into something James never intended—a weapon against suffering people.
If you have ever watched someone you love die after your church prayed for healing, please hear this carefully.
Their death does not prove that you failed to pray hard enough.
It does not prove the elders used the wrong oil.
It does not prove your loved one was secretly unworthy of God's mercy.
Scripture does not give us permission to make those accusations.
We can believe that God heals without pretending that every believer receives healing in this life.
We can pray boldly without claiming to control the outcome.
And we can trust God's goodness even when we cannot understand His providence.
That is not weak faith.
It is faith that refuses to make promises God has not authorized us to make.
There is something else in James 5 that requires careful attention.
James says:
"And if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him."
Some people read this and conclude that sickness must be caused by personal sin.
But notice that small word.
If.
James does not say that every sick person has committed some particular sin that caused their illness.
He recognizes that sin and forgiveness may be relevant, without making personal sin the universal explanation for disease.
Jesus Himself corrected that dangerous assumption.
In John 9:1–3, the disciples encountered a man who had been blind from birth.
They asked Jesus whether the man's condition resulted from his sin or his parents' sin.
Jesus rejected that explanation in this particular case.
The man's blindness was not to be understood as punishment for either person's sin.
And in Luke 13:1–5, Jesus rejected the assumption that people who suffered terrible tragedies were necessarily worse sinners than others.
Suffering is not a reliable measurement of someone's righteousness.
Yes, some sins can have physical consequences.
Yes, Scripture sometimes connects particular acts of disobedience with divine discipline.
But no, Christians are not authorized to look at a cancer patient, a disabled child, or someone battling chronic illness and declare that their suffering must be evidence of hidden sin.
That is not spiritual discernment.
It can become cruelty disguised as conviction.
And Jesus never gave His church permission to crush the wounded in His name.
James 5:16 continues:
"Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed."
Confession matters.
Repentance matters.
Restored relationships matter.
But confession is not a payment that purchases healing.
Forgiveness is grounded in God's grace through Jesus Christ.
The gospel is not that we perform enough religious actions to persuade God to love us.
The gospel is that while we were sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).
And that brings us to the most important truth in this entire discussion.
Jesus did not come merely to make sick people healthy for a few more years. He came to rescue sinners from sin and death.
Physical healing is precious.
It can be a profound expression of God's mercy.
But even people whom Jesus physically healed eventually faced death.
Lazarus walked out of his tomb in John 11.
Imagine the sound of that moment.
The grieving sisters.
The crowd standing outside.
The voice of Jesus calling a dead man by name.
And then the impossible happened.
A man who had been buried came out alive.
But Lazarus was not yet experiencing the final resurrection body promised to God's redeemed people.
His restoration to earthly life was a sign pointing beyond itself.
To Jesus.
To the One who declared in John 11:25:
"I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live."
That is the hope no disease can ultimately destroy.
A healing miracle may restore the body for a season.
But Jesus Christ offers resurrection life that death cannot finally defeat.
And the cost of that hope was not cheap.
It was paid at Calvary.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
"And with his stripes we are healed."
The Hebrew phrase is:
וּבַחֲבֻרָתוֹ נִרְפָּא־לָנוּ
Uvaḥavurato nirpa lanu.
"And by his wound, healing has come to us."
This is one of the most beautiful and frequently misunderstood statements in Scripture.
Isaiah 53 speaks of the suffering Servant bearing the sins and iniquities of others.
The context places enormous emphasis on reconciliation with God through the Servant's suffering.
Peter applies this passage to Christ in 1 Peter 2:24, where he writes about Jesus bearing our sins so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.
Peter then says:
"By whose stripes ye were healed."
The immediate emphasis is spiritual restoration through Christ's saving work.

Matthew 8:16–17 also connects Isaiah's prophecy with Jesus' ministry of physical healing, showing that His compassion for bodily suffering belongs within the broader fulfillment of the Servant's mission.
So we must hold both truths together.
Jesus' saving work addresses the full devastation brought by sin and the fall, including the ultimate defeat of sickness and death.
But Scripture does not promise that every believer will experience complete physical healing before the resurrection.
Romans 8:23 says believers still await the redemption of their bodies.
Revelation 21:4 promises a day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That is the final healing for which creation groans.
And it is coming through Jesus Christ.
Not through a bottle.
Not through a famous preacher.
Not through a perfect prayer formula.
Through the crucified and risen Lord.
So what should a Christian actually do today when someone is sick?
Take James seriously.
If you are ill, you may call upon the elders of your local church and ask them to pray over you.
They may anoint you with ordinary oil in the name of the Lord.
The biblical passage does not prescribe a special brand, price, geographical source, or secret preparation.
The elders should pray sincerely, trusting God's power and goodness rather than their own spiritual reputation.
The person receiving prayer need not pretend to possess absolute certainty about the outcome.
And the church should continue caring for that person whether recovery comes quickly, slowly, or not in this life.
There is no biblical reason to make anointing oil a commercial requirement for receiving prayer.
There is also no biblical reason to forbid the practice merely because it has sometimes been misused.

Christians from different traditions have understood aspects of James 5 differently, particularly whether the anointing is chiefly medicinal, symbolic, sacramental, or some combination of these. But the passage clearly centers the church's ministry to the sick on prayer offered in the Lord's name.

We should also remember that James specifically mentions the elders of the church. The passage does not teach that only elders may ever pray for sick people, but it does give them a particular pastoral responsibility.
And please, do not abandon appropriate medical treatment in the name of faith.
Seeking medical care is not a betrayal of trust in God.
God can work through ordinary means as well as extraordinary intervention.
You may receive prayer and take prescribed medicine.
You may ask the elders to anoint you and still undergo surgery.
You may believe in miracles and still listen carefully to qualified healthcare professionals.
Those things do not have to compete.
And when someone is suffering, the church's responsibility should not end after the oil has been applied.
Bring food.
Help with transportation.
Visit the lonely.
Assist with practical needs when possible.
Sit beside the person whose strength is failing.
Pray again tomorrow.
And if the suffering continues, do not disappear.
Because one of the saddest things a church can do is celebrate a testimony of healing while forgetting the believer who remains sick.
Jesus never taught us to love only the people whose stories end the way we hoped.
Sometimes the most Christlike thing you can do is stay beside someone when you have no explanation for their pain.
And perhaps that is why James begins with the sick person calling for the elders.
The church is not supposed to be an audience watching someone else's suffering.
It is supposed to be a family that comes near.
Now, there is one more question we must face.
What if you have been prayed over?
What if the oil was applied?
What if you confessed your sins, asked God for mercy, and still woke up in pain?
What then?
Then you keep looking to Jesus.
Not because your pain is imaginary.
Not because you must pretend everything is fine.
Not because every unanswered prayer has an explanation you can discover.
But because the gospel gives you a Savior who entered a world of suffering and did not remain distant from it.
Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb.
Jesus touched people others avoided.
Jesus heard the cries of the desperate.
Jesus endured agony in Gethsemane.
And Jesus Himself prayed:
"Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done" (Luke 22:42).
There is no shame in praying, "Father, please heal me."
There is no shame in crying.
There is no shame in saying, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief" (Mark 9:24).
But Christian faith ultimately rests not in the certainty that God will give us the outcome we desire today.
It rests in the character and saving work of Jesus Christ.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who intercedes for His people.
The One who will make all things new.
That is why the answer to our original question is yes—anointing sick believers with oil remains a biblically grounded practice for Christians today.
James gives the church no indication that his instruction was intended to expire after the apostolic generation.
We should therefore take it seriously, while recognizing that faithful Christians may differ over the precise theological meaning of the oil.
But anointing is never a substitute for the gospel.
It is never permission to exploit the desperate.
And it is never a guarantee that every illness will disappear.
The church must not turn an act of compassion into a spectacle, a business transaction, or a test of whether someone deserves God's mercy.
The sick need prayer.
They need truth.
They need care.
And above all, they need Jesus.
Maybe you began reading this article because you wanted to know whether Christians should still use anointing oil.
But perhaps somewhere along the way, another question surfaced.
Have you been seeking God's hand while keeping your heart closed to His grace?
It is possible to want a miracle without wanting the Savior.
It is possible to ask Jesus to remove pain while refusing to surrender the sin that is destroying us.
And it is possible to know religious language while remaining far from Christ.
The greatest need of the human soul is not merely to escape physical suffering.
It is to be reconciled to God.
We have all sinned (Romans 3:23).
We cannot save ourselves through rituals, offerings, church attendance, or religious performance.
But Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again.
And the call of the gospel is to repent and believe in Him.
Not to purchase His mercy.
Not to earn His forgiveness.
But to receive the grace that only He can give.
If you have been running from God, you do not have to keep running.
If you have been hiding behind religious appearances, you can come into the light.
If you have been wounded by someone who used God's name to manipulate your desperation, do not confuse that person's wrongdoing with the character of Jesus.
Come to Christ.
Bring Him the sin you have concealed.
Bring Him the grief you cannot explain.
Bring Him the fears that return when the lights go out.
And trust the Savior who receives those who come to Him in faith.
You may pray something like this:

"Lord Jesus, I confess that I am a sinner in need of Your mercy. Forgive me for trusting in myself more than in You. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to repent, to trust Your Word, and to follow You. Whether I am healed quickly, slowly, or must endure suffering, help me remain faithful. Let my hope rest in You and not in any ritual. Amen."
There is no magical power in repeating these words. Salvation is not produced by a formula. It is God's gracious gift received through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And if you are already a believer who is suffering, remember this.
Your illness has not made you less valuable to God.
Your weakness has not placed you beyond the reach of His grace.
Your unanswered questions do not surprise Him.
You may not know what tomorrow's medical report will say.
But the resurrection of Jesus gives you a hope that reaches beyond tomorrow.
And that truth deserves to be carried beyond this article.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be sitting in a hospital waiting room right now, wondering whether God has abandoned them.
Someone may be afraid to ask for prayer because they have been told their sickness is proof of hidden sin.
Someone may be spending money they cannot afford on so-called miracle products because nobody has explained what James 5 actually teaches.
But before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Have you ever prayed for healing and received an answer you did not expect?
Have you witnessed God restore someone?
Or are you still waiting, still trusting, still fighting to believe while the suffering continues?
And if God has brought you through a season of suffering, consider sharing a brief testimony. Not every testimony needs to end with a dramatic physical miracle. Sometimes a testimony is simply this:
"I was hurting, but Jesus did not abandon me."
Your words may help another believer persevere.
And if this kind of Scripture-grounded teaching has helped you, I invite you to stay connected with Gospel Warrior.

These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment more accessible, especially to people who need encouragement and teaching but may not have the means to purchase books and study materials.
And for those who believe in this mission and are able to help sustain it, there is another way to participate.
Scripture says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Giving that honors God is not produced by guilt or pressure.
It flows from love, gratitude, and a willing heart.
The gospel is not for sale.
The free resources are not a reward reserved for people who pay.
And God's love cannot be purchased through monthly payments.
Your decision to follow may help you stay connected with teaching that points you back to Scripture.
And your prayers for this ministry matter deeply.
Because the purpose is not to build a following around a human personality.
It is to point people toward Jesus Christ.
The same Jesus who welcomed the broken.
The same Jesus who called sinners to repentance.
The same Jesus who died for the ungodly.
The same Jesus who rose from the grave.
And the same Jesus who promises that one day, for those who belong to Him, death itself will be swallowed up in victory.
So yes, bring the oil when Scripture calls for it.
Call the elders.
Pray with faith.
Seek wise medical care.
Confess your sins.
Care for the suffering.
Trust the Lord.
But never mistake the sign for the Savior.

Because when the oil has been wiped away, when the prayers have ended, when the hospital room grows quiet again, and when you are left facing everything you cannot control, there is still Someone worthy of your trust.
His name is Jesus.
And if you belong to Him, even death will not have the final word over your story.
The oil may touch your skin for a moment, but only Jesus can redeem your soul for eternity.
